papers.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scientific Particle Data Compression and Rendering
papers.abstract: Large-scale particle simulations produce hundreds of millions of particles, straining storage, transfer, and interactive visualization. Existing lossy compressors such as SZ3 operate in data space and provide no guarantees on downstream visualization fidelity. We propose ParticleGS, a visualization-aware framework based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that learns a compact representation directly optimized for rendered image quality, combining (1) a multi-stage, multi-orbit training pipeline, (2) VizMapper, a lightweight network that adapts a single trained model to user-specified visualization parameters at inference time, and (3) spatial block training with KD-tree decomposition and global fine-tuning. On a 281-million-particle HACC cosmological simulation, our 8-block model reaches 30.03 dB PSNR at 65x compression, outperforming SZ3 by 5-8 dB at comparable ratios, and generalizes without tuning to additional HACC regions and a dark-matter-only FIRE-2 simulation. It renders at 662 FPS on a single GPU, over 2,300x faster than ParaView on the full particle data.
papers.title_text: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scientific Particle Data Compression and Rendering

papers.title: A GPU-Accelerated and Geometry-Aware Quantum-Classical Framework for Optimized PES Scans with CUDA-Q
papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical workloads, particularly Potential Energy Surface (PES) scans in quantum chemistry using batched VQE and QAOA, involve many structurally similar Hamiltonians differing only in coefficients. Existing warm-start and meta-optimization strategies reuse parameters between instances but still consume fixed quantum-classical resources, ignoring cross-instance structural similarities. We present OptiPESS, a GPU-accelerated runtime system for adaptive resource allocation in hybrid quantum-classical execution. OptiPESS introduces the Locality-Occupancy-Variance (LOV) metric, a lightweight, geometry-aware measure of Hamiltonian similarity, coupled with efficient alignment and Pauli-classification passes. Using LOV, OptiPESS performs distance-aware scheduling of iteration and shot budgets, predicting which instances can be skipped, quick-solved, or fully optimized. Implemented atop CUDA-Q with persistent multi-GPU execution and near-linear scaling, OptiPESS reduces classical and quantum evaluations by up to 78.3\% and wall-time by up to 74.8\% while maintaining baseline accuracy. This demonstrates how lightweight static analysis and adaptive scheduling can transform quantum-classical co-execution from fixed-budget loops into a predictive, resource-aware runtime.
papers.title_text: A GPU-Accelerated and Geometry-Aware Quantum-Classical Framework for Optimized PES Scans with CUDA-Q

papers.title: A Hardware Abstraction for Exascale Lattice Boltzmann Simulations: Rotor-Resolved Wind Farms on Aurora and LUMI
papers.abstract: Developing performance-portable lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) codes for heterogeneous hardware without extensive hardware-specific duplication is challenging. We introduce a unified hardware abstraction within the open-source OpenLB framework. By expressing models against abstract cell-level concepts, this design enables compile-time binding to platform-specific data structures and common subexpression elimination across composed operators, yielding up to 2.5-fold speedups over an unoptimized baseline. We validate this approach using a rotor-resolved, wall-modeled large-eddy simulation (WMLES) of a 32-turbine wind farm, combining LBM with Brinkman penalization, moving walls and atmospheric boundary layer inflow. This complex fluid-structure interaction executes across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs from a single-source implementation without hardware-specific modifications. At extreme scale, we execute the simulation on up to 2,048 Aurora nodes, achieving 86% weak scaling efficiency against a single node. Resolving 5.9 trillion cells at 51 trillion cell updates per second, this is the largest GPU-accelerated LBM simulation reported to date.
papers.title_text: A Hardware Abstraction for Exascale Lattice Boltzmann Simulations: Rotor-Resolved Wind Farms on Aurora and LUMI

papers.title: A Parallel Algorithm for the Construction of Partial Information Decomposition-Based Genome-Scale Networks from Single-Cell Datasets
papers.abstract: Methods for constructing gene networks from tissue-level expression data, developed over the past two decades, are being reassessed for applicability to single-cell datasets. The higher noise and sparsity of single-cell data demand more robust, computationally intensive approaches, while also requiring scalability to orders-of-magnitude larger datasets. We focus on PIDC, an information-theoretic method that produces high-quality networks from single-cell data but incurs $O(n^3)$ runtime for $n$ genes, limiting scalability even with parallelization. We present a novel sequential algorithm that reduces complexity to $O(n^2 \log n)$, along with its distributed-memory parallelization achieving $O(n^2/p + T_{sort}(n^2, p))$ time, where $p$ is the number of processors and $T_{sort}$ is the time for parallel sorting. On 64 cores, our MPI implementation achieves a 158X speedup over the existing PIDC algorithm. We further demonstrate construction of a genome-scale human gene network with 30,000 genes from 800,000 cells in 2.5 hours using 2,048 cores.
papers.title_text: A Parallel Algorithm for the Construction of Partial Information Decomposition-Based Genome-Scale Networks from Single-Cell Datasets

papers.title: A Unified Multi-Dimensional Parallel Algorithm for Communication-Avoiding SpMM
papers.abstract: Distributed sparse matrix–dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) is often bottlenecked by communication and performs poorly under irregular sparsity patterns. We propose a unified task–data parallel (TDP) framework that jointly models task decomposition and data distribution, enabling communication analysis across the SpMM design space. Within this framework, we identify two complementary 2D submodels, $mn\text{-}r_A r_B$ and $kn\text{-}c_A r_C$, with distinct sparsity-dependent communication costs, and develop a fused MNKN algorithm that partitions the sparse matrix into tiles and assigns each tile to the lower-cost submodel using lightweight sparsity-aware metrics. This design enables fine-grained dense-side communication avoidance without additional storage overhead while naturally overlapping communication and computation. Experiments on large-scale SuiteSparse matrices show performance gains on 68% of 135 matrices, including up to an order-of-magnitude speedup over 2D SUMMA and an average speedup of 2.4x over the sparsity-aware CRP baseline on 10 representative matrices. We further demonstrate its effectiveness in polynomial-filtering eigensolvers.
papers.title_text: A Unified Multi-Dimensional Parallel Algorithm for Communication-Avoiding SpMM

papers.title: Accelerating SpGEMM Through Lightweight Clustering and Cache-Aware Accumulation
papers.abstract: Sparse matrix-matrix multiplication is one of the most crucial kernels in linear algebra solvers, graph analytics, and machine learning workloads. The clustered row-row style has emerged as a favorable SpGEMM workflow because of its potentially good parallelism. However, due to frequent data movement caused by irregular memory access, existing approaches often suffer from three issues: (1) workload imbalance and prohibitive preprocessing overhead, (2) unsatisfactory data locality, and (3) inefficient accumulation strategy. To this end, we propose LeSpGEMM, a locality-enhanced SpGEMM algorithm. LeSpGEMM introduces a lightweight row-clustering method to improve spatial locality with near-linear complexity, and a cache-aware hybrid accumulation strategy to exploit data reuse across diverse sparse patterns. It further incorporates optimized kernels, including a SIMD-accelerated dense accumulator and an efficient hash-based accumulator. Experimental results on multiple platforms show that LeSpGEMM significantly outperforms six state-of-the-art implementations while maintaining low preprocessing overhead.
papers.title_text: Accelerating SpGEMM Through Lightweight Clustering and Cache-Aware Accumulation

papers.title: Arachne: Orchestrating Cascades for Efficient Text-to-Video Model Training
papers.abstract: The rising demand for AI-generated videos is fueled by advances in large-scale Text-to-Video (T2V) models, trained on extensive datasets of video clips spanning diverse resolutions and durations. To address this data heterogeneity, current training methods often use a bucketing strategy that groups samples into discrete buckets for efficiency. However, this approach struggles to scale with compute and data volumes under static parallelism schemes, such as data and sequence parallelism, leading to significant workload imbalances and hardware under-utilization. In this paper, we present Arachne, a novel training framework for efficient T2V model training at scale. Arachne decomposes the training process into fine-grained computational units, called \textit{cascades}, orchestrating their distributed execution and synchronization across the cluster through coordinated spatial and temporal optimization. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that Arachne reduces iteration time by up to 65\% over leading frameworks, exhibiting a positive scaling trend where its performance advantages amplify as training scale grows.
papers.title_text: Arachne: Orchestrating Cascades for Efficient Text-to-Video Model Training

papers.title: BaGuaLu-2: Taming Dynamic Memory Fluctuation for Efficient MoE Model Training Over 10,000 GPUs
papers.abstract: Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is the de facto architecture for scaling large language models. However, dynamic expert load imbalance causes severe memory fluctuations that degrade training efficiency. Existing systems rely on static memory provisioning: they either over-provision, leaving GPU memory idle during normal execution, or under- provision, inviting out-of-memory crashes and costly manual rollbacks when load spikes occur. To address these challenges, we propose BaGuaLu-2, a large-scale MoE training system that eliminates this dilemma through flexible provisioning. By transforming memory allocation from a static, one-time tuning choice into a continuous and fine-grained control. BaGuaLu-2 grants exact activation memory on demand for each training batch. Furthermore, it offsets any dynamic management overhead through system optimizations. BaGuaLu-2 demonstrates exceptional scalability, training a model with 1040 billion parameters across 12,288 GPUs while sustaining over 2 EFlops at 35% MFU. Compared with state-of-the-art systems, BaGuaLu-2 delivers 1.14x and 1.13x average throughput improvements over Megatron-Kuai and AdaPipe, respectively.
papers.title_text: BaGuaLu-2: Taming Dynamic Memory Fluctuation for Efficient MoE Model Training Over 10,000 GPUs

papers.title: BAHAMAS: A Control Plane for Optimization and Execution of Variational Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) suffer from unstable optimization due to temporal noise drift and static qubit mappings that distort gradient signals across iterations. We present BAHAMAS, an online control framework that stabilizes noise exposure by adaptively selecting physical mappings via consensus-based fidelity estimation, without requiring simulators, offline training, or prior executions. Across real quantum devices, BAHAMAS improves optimization reliability and supports inference-time retargeting under drift through robust, per-iteration control.
papers.title_text: BAHAMAS: A Control Plane for Optimization and Execution of Variational Quantum Circuits

papers.title: BatchFlow: Benefit-Aware Data Pipeline Allocation and Batch Reuse for Multi-Job Training
papers.abstract: Deep learning training is often limited by data pipeline throughput, reducing accelerator utilization and increasing training time and cost. This is particularly challenging in multi-tenant environments, where jobs compete for storage and CPU resources. We present BatchFlow, a data pipeline service that improves aggregate training throughput by dynamically allocating data pipeline workers across jobs. BatchFlow uses online profiling to estimate how quickly each job consumes mini-batches and how quickly workers can prepare them, then allocates workers to jobs where data supply is most likely to fall behind training demand. BatchFlow also caches prepared mini-batches for reuse across jobs, reducing repeated reads from slow storage and redundant CPU preprocessing. When cache capacity is limited, a benefit-aware policy determines which mini-batches to prefetch and retain. Across multi-job workloads, BatchFlow increases aggregate training throughput by up to 3.8× and cost efficiency by up to 2.1× relative to prior systems.
papers.title_text: BatchFlow: Benefit-Aware Data Pipeline Allocation and Batch Reuse for Multi-Job Training

papers.title: BatchMine: Accelerating Approximate Graph Pattern Mining via Batch Processing
papers.abstract: Approximate graph pattern mining, as a fundamental technique in graph analysis, has been widely applied in machine learning, biomedical research, and social network analysis. However, existing solutions still face significant challenges in efficiency and scalability when dealing with complex pattern graphs or giant data graphs. To address these limitations, we introduce BatchMine, an out-of-core system for approximate graph pattern mining. BatchMine leverages three key techniques: (1) a partition-based estimation method to accelerate convergence; (2) a batch-processing framework with adaptive refinement to enhance external-memory access locality and improve convergence efficiency; and (3) a hybrid data layout that balances sampling efficiency and storage overhead. To the best of our knowledge, BatchMine is the first graph pattern mining system capable of handling graphs exceeding main memory capacity, enabling mining on graphs with nearly 100 billion edges on a single machine within 1,000 seconds. Extensive experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of BatchMine.
papers.title_text: BatchMine: Accelerating Approximate Graph Pattern Mining via Batch Processing

papers.title: BidKV: Utility-Guided Preemption Scheduling for KV-Pressure LLM Serving
papers.abstract: When key-value (KV) cache demand exceeds GPU memory in online large language model (LLM) serving, engines reclaim active requests' cache. Poor victim selection increases recomputation and time to first token (TTFT). We present BidKV, a utility-guided policy that ranks victims by recoverable capacity and estimated disruption cost. BidKV integrates with vLLM and SGLang through a portable adapter that reuses native preemption. With Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and ShareGPT traces, BidKV reduces 95th-percentile TTFT by over 90% and improves 300 ms service-level objective (SLO) attainment by 14.8 percentage points over vLLM's native policy. On SGLang, it reduces 95th-percentile TTFT by 94.6% and improves SLO attainment by 38.8 percentage points over native least-recently-used eviction. Source code is available at https://github.com/CGCL-codes/BidKV.
papers.title_text: BidKV: Utility-Guided Preemption Scheduling for KV-Pressure LLM Serving

papers.title: BitIR: Cross-Architecture Fault Injection for Resilience Analysis of Heterogeneous GPU Applications
papers.abstract: Modern GPU-based HPC systems rely on heterogeneous vendor stacks, yet resilience studies are largely limited to single architectures, leaving it unclear how faults behave across different GPU backends. We present \emph{BitIR}, a cross-architecture fault injection framework that injects deterministic single-bit faults at the LLVM IR level, ensuring semantically equivalent perturbations prior to backend lowering and enabling direct cross-vendor comparison across NVIDIA, Intel, and AMD GPUs. We evaluate BitIR on three production supercomputers -- Polaris (ALCF, NVIDIA A100), Aurora (ALCF, Intel GPU Max 1550), and Frontier (OLCF, AMD Instinct MI250X) -- representing the full spectrum of current leadership-class GPU architectures. Using representative heterogeneous benchmarks, we conduct large-scale injection campaigns across all three systems and classify outcomes into masked results, silent data corruptions (SDCs), and failures. Our results show that identical faults produce markedly different behaviors across vendors: Intel most often masks faults but exhibits more hangs when faults escape masking, NVIDIA exposes more detectable hard failures, and AMD alternates between SDC-dominant and failure-dominant behavior depending on the benchmark and fault site. These findings demonstrate that resilience is not backend-invariant, underscoring the need for backend-aware and workload-aware fault mitigation.
papers.title_text: BitIR: Cross-Architecture Fault Injection for Resilience Analysis of Heterogeneous GPU Applications

papers.title: BlockMGARD: Accelerating Adaptive Scientific Data Reduction with Region-of-Interest Error Control on GPUs
papers.abstract: The growing scale of scientific data makes lossy compression essential for reducing data volume under controllable error. Transformation-based compressors using multilevel decomposition, such as MGARD, achieve strong compression ratios but map poorly to GPU architectures. We propose BlockMGARD, an adaptive, Region-of-Interest (ROI)-supported GPU lossy compressor, with four contributions: (1) an In-cache Block decomposition leveraging GPU on-chip memory and constant lookup tables to accelerate decomposition; (2) a hybrid hierarchy combining In-cache Block and global decomposition to balance speed and compression ratio; (3) an end-to-end pipeline with fine-grained ROI error control for feature preservation; and (4) an evaluation against state-of-the-art methods on five real-world datasets. Compared to MGARD-X, BlockMGARD achieves up to 4.2x and 9.1x higher compression and decompression throughput, and up to 8.63x higher compression ratio than uniform-tolerance baselines under ROI-aware error control. Across four GPUs, BlockMGARD achieves near-ideal linear scaling and up to 1.58x I/O cost reduction over MGARD-X.
papers.title_text: BlockMGARD: Accelerating Adaptive Scientific Data Reduction with Region-of-Interest Error Control on GPUs

papers.title: BMS2: Fast Batched Subgraph Matching on GPUs with Structure-Aware Scheduling
papers.abstract: Batched matching is widely used in drug discovery, software analysis, and social network analysis. Its core operation, subgraph matching, is an NP-complete graph algorithm that has been optimized in the HPC field for decades. As for batching scenario, we find that current subgraph matching systems are unable to leverage the common structure patterns of real-world graphs, thereby missing potential optimization opportunities. In this paper, we propose BMS2, a batched matching system with structure-aware scheduling. BMS2 incorporates these intrinsic properties into previous general filter-join strategy: (1) in the filter phase, BMS2 utilizes the presence information of special structure for early termination; (2) in the join phase, we exploit the similarity of batched queries to reuse matching results of common structure. Experiments demonstrate that BMS2 can achieve an order of magnitude performance improvement on GPUs compared to the state-of-the-art with the ability to process two orders of magnitude larger dataset.
papers.title_text: BMS2: Fast Batched Subgraph Matching on GPUs with Structure-Aware Scheduling

papers.title: Bridging Precision and Performance Gaps: Scientific Computing on AI-Oriented Architectures
papers.abstract: The rapid rise of AI-oriented accelerators has reshaped compute systems around low-precision tensor engines, raising a practical question for the HPC community: Under what conditions can such hardware support scientific workloads that demand numerical robustness, irregular memory access, and scalability? Using the Ascend 910 NPU series as a representative tensor-centric platform, we characterize precision, execution, and memory-hierarchy bottlenecks that hinder the direct deployment of scientific codes. From this characterization, we develop and evaluate workload-specific mappings that combine heterogeneous execution, mixed-precision numerical formulations, hierarchical memory orchestration, and communication–computation overlap. Evaluations spanning kernels, numerical solvers, quantum simulation, and Monte Carlo applications show that AI-native NPUs can achieve numerical robustness, competitive performance, and satisfactory scalability when these constraints are addressed in a coordinated manner. Our results provide a state-of-the-practice case study of how scientific workloads can be adapted to tensor-centric architectures, while distinguishing transferable optimization principles from Ascend-specific implementation details.
papers.title_text: Bridging Precision and Performance Gaps: Scientific Computing on AI-Oriented Architectures

papers.title: BTC-TC: Exact GPU Triangle Counting with Hybrid Bit Tensor Cores and CUDA Cores
papers.abstract: Triangle counting is fundamental to graph analytics, yet GPUs face a tension between exact, irregular adjacency-list intersection and regular, inaccurate FP16 Tensor Core execution. ToT's FP16 pipeline is incorrect on 12 of 36 inputs and requires pre-kernel symbolic matching. We observe that semantic alignment alone is insufficient under heterogeneous mask density. We present BTC-TC, an exact system built around binary MMA. AND-popcount implements common-neighbor counting with 32-bit accumulation and enables online block matching. Because mask density varies, BTC-TC combines multi-granularity Bit-BSR with two-level adaptivity: it selects block geometry per graph, dispatches dense blocks to Bit Tensor Cores, and routes sparse blocks to CUDA cores. Across 36 inputs and 12 baselines on RTX PRO 6000, BTC-TC achieves the lowest post-clean end-to-end time on every input, with 1.92x geometric-mean kernel and 8.0x end-to-end speedups over ToT. It matches CPU ground truth on every input and maintains the gains on H100 and A800.
papers.title_text: BTC-TC: Exact GPU Triangle Counting with Hybrid Bit Tensor Cores and CUDA Cores

papers.title: Characterizing the Scalability and Performance of Large-Scale AI Training Under Multi-Tenancy
papers.abstract: Characterising AI workload performance on modern HPC systems requires understanding both their scalability in isolation and their behaviour under concurrent execution. However, the interplay among parallelisation strategies, network congestion, compute capability, and interconnect technologies remains poorly understood. This work investigates the performance and scalability of AI models up to 2400 GPUs. We quantify the communication overheads and their impact across different interconnects by evaluating scale-up, scale-out, and rack-scale configurations under multiple allocation schemes. Finally, we study how multiple concurrent training jobs interfere with each other by designing a realistic noise model. We design a benchmark suite of AI models to evaluate the performance of five distinct parallelisation strategies across different supercomputing clusters, including Alps, Leonardo, LUMI, JUPITER, NVL72 GB300, and DGX A100. Our work provides a systematic characterization of the scalability and execution efficiency of distributed AI training, while offering key insights into performance behavior under realistic multi-tenant scenarios.
papers.title_text: Characterizing the Scalability and Performance of Large-Scale AI Training Under Multi-Tenancy

papers.title: Chisa: Dynamic Logical Way Partitioning for Efficient Caching in Sparse Accelerators
papers.abstract: Sparse tensor computations are memory-bound, making on-chip data reuse critical to sparse accelerator performance. Guided cache replacement derives lookahead information from structural relationships between operand tensors, but its effectiveness hinges on the prefetch observation window in SRAM. Under constrained SRAM, the window is inevitably small and guidance becomes noisy or misleading—precisely when caching matters most. We propose Chisa, a dynamic logical way partitioning scheme for sparse accelerator caches. Inspired by victim caches, Chisa integrates buffer semantics into cache sets: a single role bit lets each way dynamically serve as a logical cache or buffer way without data migration, so mistakenly evicted blocks can be rescued upon reuse. Chisa further incorporates Jaccard similarity-based initialization and rescue rate-based runtime adaptation. On real-world sparse matrices, Chisa achieves geometric mean speedups of 1.23x and 1.27x over the state of the art on SpMSpM and SpMM, respectively, peaking at 4.46x and 4.64x.
papers.title_text: Chisa: Dynamic Logical Way Partitioning for Efficient Caching in Sparse Accelerators

papers.title: CoCoDiff: Optimizing Collective Communications for Distributed Diffusion Transformer Inference Under Ulysses Sequence Parallelism
papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are increasingly adopted in scientific computing, yet growing model sizes and resolutions make distributed multi-GPU inference essential. Ulysses sequence parallelism scales DiT inference but introduces frequent all-to-all collectives that dominate latency. Overlapping these with computation is difficult due to tight data dependencies, large messages, and asymmetric interconnect bandwidths. We introduce CoCoDiff, a distributed DiT inference engine exploiting two observations: (1) V requires only linear projection while Q/K need additional normalization and RoPE, enabling overlap of V's communication with Q/K computation; (2) adjacent denoising steps produce similar tensors, yielding temporal redundancy. CoCoDiff introduces three mechanisms: Tile-Aware Parallel All-to-all (TAPA) decomposes collectives into topology-aligned phases; V-First scheduling hides V's communication behind Q/K computation; and V-Major selective communication transmits only active projections on slow interconnects. On Aurora with four DiT models across 1–8 nodes (up to 96 Intel GPU tiles), CoCoDiff achieves an average speedup of 3.6×, peaking at 8.4×.
papers.title_text: CoCoDiff: Optimizing Collective Communications for Distributed Diffusion Transformer Inference Under Ulysses Sequence Parallelism

papers.title: Communication Avoiding Parallel Sketching via Sparse Subspace Embeddings
papers.abstract: This paper considers sketching via sparse subspace embeddings that are commonly employed in randomized algorithms due to their efficiency when applied to large-scale matrices. We introduce lower bounds on communication and design optimal algorithms for sketching large-scale matrices using sparse random embeddings. We consider different matrix dimensions and aspect ratios that are relevant for scientific computing and machine learning applications. We demonstrate the strong and weak scalability of these algorithms on both CPU and GPU architectures.
papers.title_text: Communication Avoiding Parallel Sketching via Sparse Subspace Embeddings

papers.title: Constructing a Job-Centric Frontier Telemetry Dataset to Accelerate HPC Operations, Systems, and Energy Research
papers.abstract: Comprehensive analysis of high-performance computing (HPC) systems requires linking workload execution to system behavior. This kind of analysis is vital for diagnosing performance issues, managing capacity, detecting anomalous workloads, and understanding how applications interact with system hardware. However, node telemetry data and job scheduler records are collected and analyzed in isolation and application identification requires a directed effort. We present a job-centric telemetry dataset that unifies scheduler job records with node-level measurements, enabling direct association between workloads and their corresponding power, thermal, and performance characteristics. This dataset, which spans two years of Frontier operations, aims to support a wide range of research and operational applications, including workload characterization, system analysis, and anomaly detection. This paper describes the dataset curation process, including data collection, normalization, and association of telemetry with individual job metadata. To enable further study, the dataset will be published alongside this paper for use by the HPC community.
papers.title_text: Constructing a Job-Centric Frontier Telemetry Dataset to Accelerate HPC Operations, Systems, and Energy Research

papers.title: COPPER: Improving DRAM Reliability with Low Overheads via Cooperative Parallelized Error-Correcting Codes
papers.abstract: DRAM scaling increases fault rates, motivating stronger and more efficient error correction. However, the transparency between on-die ECC (OD-ECC) in DRAM and rank-level ECC (RL-ECC) in the memory controller introduces substantial storage, reliability, and performance overheads. We propose COPPER, a cooperative ECC mechanism that improves reliability with low performance and area overheads. COPPER exploits the fixed mapping between DRAM data arrays and interface pins to convey a crafted error-location hint from OD-ECC to the memory controller, enabling parallel rank-level cross-checking and decoding without stalling memory transfers. We further propose POD-RMW, which provably parallelizes OD-ECC operations during read-modify-write. Our evaluations show that COPPER incurs only 0.007% DRAM-chip area and at most 0.001% CPU area. With 19.5% storage overhead, COPPER reduces DUE and SDC rates by up to 15x and 430x, respectively, while improving performance by up to 2.1x over prior cooperative ECC approaches under high fault rates.
papers.title_text: COPPER: Improving DRAM Reliability with Low Overheads via Cooperative Parallelized Error-Correcting Codes

papers.title: CoreFlow: Context-Centric Resource Management for LLM-Based Agentic Workflows
papers.abstract: The rise of agentic workflows, which coordinate multiple LLM-based agents to tackle complex tasks, has shifted the LLM serving toward a multi-step, context-driven execution paradigm. This shift introduces highly skewed context-length distributions and agent-specific KV cache-reuse patterns in LLM workloads, challenging existing resource management systems that remain oblivious to these characteristics. This paper introduces CoreFlow, a context-centric resource management system tailored for the distinct execution patterns of agentic workflows. CoreFlow incorporates three key designs: (1) hierarchical performance modeling, which captures the effects of context-length variance and imbalanced cache reuse inherent in context-driven execution; (2) dual-level resource optimization, combining workflow-level allocation to distribute resources across agents with agent-level partitioning to isolate requests with heterogeneous context lengths; and (3) adaptive cache management, which aligns cache placement with resource partitioning while minimizing cache-swap overhead. Evaluations on representative workflows demonstrate that CoreFlow reduces end-to-end latency by 57.6% and improves workflow throughput by 63.1%.
papers.title_text: CoreFlow: Context-Centric Resource Management for LLM-Based Agentic Workflows

papers.title: Cross-Layer Energy Analysis of Multimodal Training on Grace Hopper Superchips
papers.abstract: Multimodal deep learning models enable joint learning across heterogeneous data sources, including text, images, and video, but their rapid scaling introduces significant memory and communication bottlenecks. As model sizes and sequence lengths increase, training performance becomes increasingly impacted by data movement rather than computation. Frameworks such as DeepSpeed mitigate these challenges through CPU offloading, activation checkpointing, and communication optimizations. However, these techniques introduce additional system activity, which may affect energy efficiency. Meanwhile, tightly integrated heterogeneous architectures, such as the NVIDIA Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip, provide high-bandwidth CPU-GPU interconnects and unified memory, thereby reducing data transfer overhead. In this work, we present a cross-layer analysis of energy and performance trade-offs in multimodal training on GH200 systems, explicitly characterizing the interactions between application, runtime, and hardware layers. Leveraging high-bandwidth CPU-GPU interconnects, our results show that energy efficiency is primarily governed by data movement and overlap rather than raw compute utilization, and that configurations optimized for runtime are not necessarily optimal for energy. Based on these findings, we distill a set of actionable guidelines for practitioners that demonstrate how to balance offloading strategies, sequence parallelism, and hardware-aware scheduling to achieve energy-efficient training. Our results demonstrate that leveraging high-bandwidth CPU-GPU interconnects enables offloading strategies and sequence parallelism, achieving a strong balance among energy efficiency, runtime performance, and computational throughput, providing practical guidelines for efficient multimodal training on modern heterogeneous systems.
papers.title_text: Cross-Layer Energy Analysis of Multimodal Training on Grace Hopper Superchips

papers.title: DeepSim: SOL-Based Explainable GPU Performance Projection with Multi-Task Learning
papers.abstract: Accurate kernel-level GPU performance projection is essential for early-stage architecture design when target hardware is unavailable and only high-level specifications are known. Existing methods face a trade-off: simulators reveal bottlenecks but are slow and require unavailable hardware details, while analytical and end-to-end learning models are efficient yet rely on idealized assumptions and provide limited explainability. We present DeepSim, an explainable GPU performance projection framework for single-GPU kernels that learns unit-level speed-of-light (SOL) ratios to calibrate bottleneck pressure using multi-task learning. Given target chip specifications and kernel traffic from existing GPUs, DeepSim constructs idealized limiters, predicts per-unit SOL ratios, and maps them to practical limiters reflecting target-chip behavior. Using this representation, DeepSim infers dominant bottlenecks, classifies workloads, and estimates execution time. Across 290K samples and 284 kernels spanning NVIDIA Ampere, Ada, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs, DeepSim achieves 12.29% mean absolute percentage error on held-out B200 and 14.78% on unseen kernels.
papers.title_text: DeepSim: SOL-Based Explainable GPU Performance Projection with Multi-Task Learning

papers.title: Demonstrating the Neuromorphic Advantage on Stochastic Dynamics in Turbulent Flows
papers.abstract: Graphics processing units (GPUs) excel at workloads dependent on linear algebra, covering a wide range of topics like artificial intelligence and quantum mechanics. However, in workloads that are not well captured by linear algebra, such as probabilistic systems, GPUs may not provide optimal performance. In this work, we demonstrate a neuromorphic advantage in energy efficiency for simulating turbulent flows with stochastic methods. We observe energy savings across the board and runtime speed-up for some methods when comparing a neuromorphic platform to equivalent workloads on GPU and CPU. Specifically, our neuromorphic implementation achieves 1.52x speed-up and 37.46x less energy consumption, compared to a GPU running the same 1.5 million random walks over discretized space. For 100,000 walks in continuous space, GPU outperforms neuromorphic in execution time but consumes 2.37x more energy. As the technological landscape for neuromorphic systems rapidly evolves, their performance relative to current hardware is likely to significantly improve.
papers.title_text: Demonstrating the Neuromorphic Advantage on Stochastic Dynamics in Turbulent Flows

papers.title: DiffSpec: Accelerating Long Sequence Generation with Differential Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Long sequence generation is a critical workload for large language model (LLM) inference, but its high computational cost limits scalable deployment. Existing speculative decoding methods accelerate inference by verifying multiple draft tokens per step, yet uniform speculation concentrates failures in late decoding stages, where marginal payoff is highest, reducing overall speedup. We propose DiffSpec, a differential speculative decoding framework that adapts speculation to position-specific utility. At the algorithmic level, DiffSpec employs utility-guided draft construction with relevance-aware key-value (KV) selection and adaptive draft tree construction, improving candidate quality in high-impact regions. At the system level, a differential speculative execution engine supports utility-adaptive speculation via reuse-aware KV residency and topology-aware fused verification, handling irregular KV cache accesses and heterogeneous workloads. Experiments on four NVIDIA H100 GPUs with sequences up to 128K tokens show end-to-end speedups of 7.72×, 3.45×, and 2.36× over EAGLE-3, TriForce, and MagicDec, respectively.
papers.title_text: DiffSpec: Accelerating Long Sequence Generation with Differential Speculative Decoding

papers.title: DistFP: Scaling Floating-Point In-Network AllReduce on In-Path Programmable Switches
papers.abstract: Floating-point (FP) gradient aggregation can bottleneck distributed machine learning training. In-network aggregation (INA) can reduce this overhead by aggregating gradients in network switches. However, current in-path programmable switches based on the protocol-independent switch architecture (PISA) lack native FP support. Existing work emulates FP INA with integer arithmetic units, consuming substantial pipeline resources and limiting aggregation parallelism. We present DistFP, a host-switch co-designed system for high-parallelism FP AllReduce on PISA-based in-path programmable switches. Its key idea is a state-dependency decomposition: DistFP moves worker-local functions to the host while retaining cross-worker collective functions in the switch, allowing more concurrent switch aggregation instances under a fixed resource budget. On a real Tofino 1-based prototype, DistFP achieves 1.3x and 6.7x higher FP32 aggregation throughput than NCCL Ring and FPISA, respectively. In our end-to-end training evaluation, DistFP improves performance by up to 1.14x over NCCL Ring.
papers.title_text: DistFP: Scaling Floating-Point In-Network AllReduce on In-Path Programmable Switches

papers.title: Distributed Variational Quantum Linear Solver
papers.abstract: VQLS is a promising hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for solving linear systems Ax=b, but its practical deployment is hindered by the massive circuit execution overhead required when encoding arbitrary matrices via linear combination of unitaries (LCU) decomposition. Evaluating the VQLS cost function requires quadratic scaling requirement with the LCU terms, resulting in tens of thousands of circuits per iteration and millions of executions across a full optimization trajectory. To address this, we present a scalable, distributed implementation of VQLS that exploits the embarrassingly parallel structure of the gradient-free-based cost function using NVIDIA CUDA-Q conjunction with multi-node distribution for HPC system. Benchmarking on the Perlmutter supercomputer, we validated the VQLS algorithm with a sample tridiagonal Toeplitz and a canonical Hele-Shaw fluid flow problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate near ideal strong scaling and high efficiency weak scaling performance. We also used Nsight to benchmark the distributed framework to explore ideal concurrency.
papers.title_text: Distributed Variational Quantum Linear Solver

papers.title: DNoF: Rearchitecting the Collaborative I/O Processing Stack Between CPU and DPU for NVMe Over Fabrics
papers.abstract: To reduce the overhead associated with transferring large volumes of data from storage to the CPU in data-intensive applications, data centers integrate data processing units (DPUs) to manage NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) remote storage access. However, current heterogeneous DPU and CPU system architectures for NVMe-oF face challenges of limited flexibility and suboptimal utilization of bandwidth and computational resources. In this paper, we present DNoF, a collaborative I/O processing stack for DPU and CPU in NVMe-oF systems, and implement it in a real-world environment. DNoF explores collaboration strategies between the DPU and CPU, achieving near-optimal system performance for NVMe-oF remote access under various workloads and delivering more than a 2x throughput improvement compared to DPU-only NVMe-oF.
papers.title_text: DNoF: Rearchitecting the Collaborative I/O Processing Stack Between CPU and DPU for NVMe Over Fabrics

papers.title: Do We Need Tensor Cores for Stencil Computations?
papers.abstract: Stencil computation constitutes a cornerstone of scientific computing, serving as a critical kernel in domains ranging from fluid dynamics to weather simulation. While stencil computations are conventionally regarded as memory-bound and thus unsuitable for compute-centric Tensor Cores, recent empirical studies have demonstrated significant speedups after applying Tensor Cores, forming an apparent contradiction. This paper resolves this contradiction by conducting a systematic performance analysis of stencil computations on Tensor Cores. We begin by revisiting the adaptation of stencils onto Tensor Cores, quantifying the computational redundancy introduced by the transformations required to satisfy hardware constraints. These metrics are subsequently integrated into an enhanced performance model that explicitly accounts for the arithmetic intensity shifts driven by temporal fusion. Guided by this formulation, we derive analytical criteria to determine the suitability of Tensor Cores for varying stencil workloads. By classifying operational regions, we identify the specific \textit{sweet spot} for effective acceleration and further demonstrate how Sparse Tensor Cores expand this profitable design space. Extensive evaluations on NVIDIA GPUs across SOTA implementations, including DRStencil, EBISU, ConvStencil, and SPIDER, validate our performance model and analytical criteria. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in guiding stencil performance optimization.
papers.title_text: Do We Need Tensor Cores for Stencil Computations?

papers.title: DOLPHIN: Scalable Disk-RAM-GPU Pipelined Training for Massive Temporal GNNs
papers.abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (T-GNNs) play a key role in modeling dynamic graphs by learning representations that capture evolving structures and interactions. However, scaling T-GNNs remains challenging, as massive real-world graphs and complex temporal dependencies incur prohibitive runtime and memory costs. Existing systems often preload entire datasets into RAM and rely on RAM-GPU pipelines, suffering from batch-boundary pipeline bubbles, thereby limiting throughput. In this paper, we present DOLPHIN, a scalable Disk-RAM-GPU pipelined system for massive T-GNNs. DOLPHIN groups training batches into chunks and incorporates two key techniques: an I/O-efficient feature window scheduler for just-in-time Disk-to-RAM chunk provisioning, and a dependency-graph–based parallel execution plan that improves GPU utilization while preserving model quality. Together, these techniques improve pipeline efficiency across the Disk-RAM-GPU memory hierarchy and computation phases. Experiments on six real-world graphs show DOLPHIN delivers up to 21.07x faster training and reduces RAM usage by up to 92.04% compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.title_text: DOLPHIN: Scalable Disk-RAM-GPU Pipelined Training for Massive Temporal GNNs

papers.title: Double-Precision Matrix Multiplication Emulation via Ozaki-II Scheme with FP8 Quantization
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a method for emulating double-precision general matrix--matrix multiplication (DGEMM), a fundamental and performance-critical kernel in many high-performance computing applications. Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II are established DGEMM emulation schemes via low-precision matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA) units. For the Ozaki-I scheme, INT8-, FP8-, and FP16-based implementations have been proposed, all of which can be realized based on the same underlying algorithmic structure. In contrast, although INT8-based implementations of the Ozaki-II scheme have been reported, the original algorithm cannot be directly adapted to exploit FP8 MMA units. In several recent architectures, such as NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra and NVIDIA Rubin, INT8 performance has been reduced, making reliance on INT8 alone insufficient. Therefore, we introduce a novel technique to demonstrate DGEMM emulation based on the Ozaki-II scheme that operates on FP8 MMA units. Compared to the FP8-based Ozaki-I scheme, our method significantly reduces the computational cost and enables efficient FP64 emulation.
papers.title_text: Double-Precision Matrix Multiplication Emulation via Ozaki-II Scheme with FP8 Quantization

papers.title: DySpin: A Plug-and-Play Library Advancing Dynamic Sparse Long-Context Inference
papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is constrained by the memory-bandwidth and capacity demands of the key-value (KV) cache. Existing sparse methods typically use fixed per-head token budgets, overlooking variations in runtime demand. Moreover, since they retain all tokens in memory, these methods do not alleviate GPU memory capacity constraints. To overcome these limitations, we present DySpin, a plug-and-play library for dynamic sparse long-context inference. Its training-free runtime allocator dynamically adjusts token budgets to preserve important tokens and improve accuracy. To address the resulting workload imbalance, FastEstimate fuses token-importance evaluation and selection to generate scheduling indices that guide a specialized decoding attention kernel for fine-grained load balancing. DySpin further employs six-bit KV cache quantization and a novel packing format that enables register-level parallel unpacking and dequantization, reducing both dequantization overhead and memory footprint. DySpin integrates with existing sparse frameworks, improving accuracy while reducing long-context inference latency and KV cache memory usage.
papers.title_text: DySpin: A Plug-and-Play Library Advancing Dynamic Sparse Long-Context Inference

papers.title: eFaaS: A Lightweight, Kernel-Bypass Serverless Framework for HPC Workloads
papers.abstract: HPC workflows are growing in scale and complexity, demanding elastic resource provisioning and fine-grained parallel execution. While serverless computing is conceptually well-suited due to its on-demand model, existing frameworks are primarily designed for lightweight, event-driven workloads, leading to fundamental mismatches in highly concurrent HPC scenarios. In such workloads, large numbers of function instances must be created simultaneously, introducing significant startup and communication overhead. Kernel-dependent mechanisms—such as cgroups, namespaces, and the network stack—become bottlenecks: instance initialization triggers heavy lock contention, while cross-node communication incurs additional costs from data copying, serialization, and context switching. To address these issues, we propose eFaaS, a serverless architecture tailored for HPC. By leveraging eBPF, eFaaS enables lock-free isolation and zero-copy communication, minimizing kernel overhead. Experimental results show that eFaaS maintains stable performance under extreme concurrency, significantly reduces long-tail latency, and achieves end-to-end speedups of 1.27×–3.74× across representative HPC workflows.
papers.title_text: eFaaS: A Lightweight, Kernel-Bypass Serverless Framework for HPC Workloads

papers.title: Efficient Serving for Agentic LLM Workflows via Micro-Task-Level Parallelism
papers.abstract: Agentic large language model (LLM) workflows leverage the advanced capabilities of LLMs to instantiate a multi-agent paradigm, where each LLM invocation constitutes an agentic task. Existing optimizations rely on coarse-grained task-level scheduling, which fails to exploit fine-grained parallelism within the workflow, leading to resource underutilization and bursty latency. In this paper, we present Grape, a full-stack LLM system for serving agentic LLM workflows that fully exploits micro-task (μTask)-level parallelism. On the frontend, Grape proposes the TaskFlow abstraction to provide a declarative interface for workflow orchestration. Subsequently, Grape decomposes tasks represented in TaskFlow into fine-grained μTasks that expose the parallelism within the workflow. For the LLM engine, Grape adopts a μTasks-aware scheduling policy with SLO-derived constraints to ensure low-latency execution with improved resource utilization. Moreover, Grape also proposes a dedicated memory management mechanism to alleviate KV Cache memory pressure. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of Grape over state-of-the-art solutions.
papers.title_text: Efficient Serving for Agentic LLM Workflows via Micro-Task-Level Parallelism

papers.title: EMO: Energy Efficiency Modeling and Optimization for AI Workloads
papers.abstract: The massive energy consumption of GPU-accelerated AI workloads challenges sustainable computing. We observe that execution asynchrony (e.g., CPU-GPU, concurrent streams, multi-GPU) creates slack, allowing non-critical kernels to run at lower frequencies to save energy without impacting end-to-end latency. However, existing approaches fail to simultaneously achieve workload generality and fine-grained slack discovery, while high-fidelity modeling incurs prohibitive overhead. We present EMO, a lightweight framework exploiting these fine-grained opportunities. First, to identify where to optimize, EMO constructs a low-level dependency graph capturing asynchrony and performs what-if timing analysis to precisely identify slack windows. Second, to determine how to optimize, EMO introduces dependency-aware kernel packing. It aggregates kernels to preserve critical paths while collapsing redundant details, enabling high-fidelity latency-energy modeling with minimal profiling cost. Finally, EMO combines graph analysis and pack-level models to formulate energy optimization as a constrained combinatorial problem, efficiently solving for optimal frequency policies under given latency targets. Evaluations show EMO reduces energy consumption by 15%--28% with only 2%--5% performance loss and negligible overhead.
papers.title_text: EMO: Energy Efficiency Modeling and Optimization for AI Workloads

papers.title: EmuGEMM: Fused Tensor Core Kernels for Precision Emulation in Matrix Multiplication
papers.abstract: Modern GPUs devote an increasing silicon budget to low-precision matrix-multiplication units, widening the precision-throughput gap for scientific computing workloads. Ozaki Schemes I and II offer an alternative by reconstructing high-precision general matrix multiplication (GEMM) from low-precision operations, yet existing implementations leave substantial performance untapped. In particular, intermediate results are repeatedly materialized in global memory, making data movement the dominant bottleneck. We present EmuGEMM, fused integer Tensor Core kernels for NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that eliminate redundant memory round-trips in both Ozaki schemes. Using Scheme I, EmuGEMM sustains up to 1,639 Top/s on Hopper (83% of INT8 peak) and 3,654 Top/s on Blackwell (81%). For large matrices, EmuGEMM surpasses cuBLAS TF32 throughput by up to 1.4x on Hopper and 1.7x on Blackwell, at comparable accuracy. Using Scheme II, EmuGEMM extends to complex arithmetic and outperforms cuBLAS ZGEMM by up to 2.3x on Hopper and 5.5x on Blackwell.
papers.title_text: EmuGEMM: Fused Tensor Core Kernels for Precision Emulation in Matrix Multiplication

papers.title: End-to-End Modeling and Trace-Driven Replay for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Supercomputing
papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical applications increasingly execute as multi-stage workflows spanning HPC nodes, simulators, workflow runtimes, network services, and remote quantum backends. Evaluating such applications is difficult because their end-to-end critical path crosses heterogeneous components with incompatible observability and control interfaces, making reported results hard to reproduce, compare, and extrapolate. We present QTrace, an end-to-end methodology for performance analysis of hybrid quantum-classical workloads. QTrace combines a unified cross-layer tracing schema with a dependency-aware, trace-driven replay engine that preserves workflow causality while enabling controlled perturbation of backend latency, scheduling policy, and reliability-related effects. This supports both faithful reproduction of observed executions and systematic "what-if" studies for future quantum-accelerated systems. We evaluate QTrace on representative iterative and adaptive workloads across simulator-backed and remote-backend settings. The results show that QTrace reconstructs workflow behavior with high fidelity, reproduces observed executions with low replay error, and exposes bottlenecks that are often hidden by backend-centric metrics alone.
papers.title_text: End-to-End Modeling and Trace-Driven Replay for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Supercomputing

papers.title: Evaluation and Optimization of Communication Compression for 10K-GPU LLM Training
papers.abstract: Collective communication is critical for scaling large language model (LLM) training to megascale GPU clusters. However, communication becomes a major bottleneck limiting scalability. Existing approaches improve bandwidth utilization but are constrained by the physical network in large-scale clusters. Communication compression reduces data volume and offers a way to break the communication wall, yet its performance and accuracy at extreme scale remain unclear. To bridge this gap, we present the first systematic study of communication compression across scales up to 10K GPUs, showing that it maintains accuracy but suffers from limited performance gains due to bandwidth hierarchy limitations, weak communication scaling, and limited resource awareness. We enhance the co-design of communication and compression with a hierarchical method that restructures communication compression, adapts communication algorithms to each scale, and tunes network resource allocation. Our approach achieves up to 5.87x communication improvement and 1.73x end-to-end training speedup on Llama3 models at 10,240 GPUs.
papers.title_text: Evaluation and Optimization of Communication Compression for 10K-GPU LLM Training

papers.title: Every Microsecond Matters: Achieving Near-Speed-of-Light Latency in GPU Collectives
papers.abstract: GPU collective communication is typically optimized for bandwidth, yet many emerging workloads are increasingly limited by latency. Long-context decode-heavy large language model (LLM) inference is a prime example, where serving large models requires multiple GPUs, and many small collectives lie directly on the critical path of token generation. Therefore, even microsecond of overhead can impact performance and cost. In this work, we study how to approach the hardware Speed-of-Light (SoL) lower bound for GPU collectives within a scale-up network. We identify key principles for near-optimal designs, including barrier-free synchronization and efficient use of symmetric memory and multicast. Building on NCCL's device-side API, we develop low-latency interfaces for constructing custom collective kernels and use them to implement new symmetric collectives in NCCL. Microbenchmarks show substantial latency reductions for small and medium messages, reducing overhead to within 7% of the absolute SoL lower bound. When integrated into real applications, these kernels improve inter-token latency and throughput in LLM inference and accelerate cuSOLVERMp, demonstrating benefits for both AI inference and traditional HPC workloads.
papers.title_text: Every Microsecond Matters: Achieving Near-Speed-of-Light Latency in GPU Collectives

papers.title: Expert-as-a-Service: Towards Efficient, Scalable, and Robust Large-Scale MoE Serving
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models challenge serving infrastructures with dynamic, sparse expert utilization, causing instability on conventional systems designed for dense architectures. We propose EaaS, a novel serving system to enable efficient, scalable, and robust MoE deployment. Our system disaggregates MoE modules into independent, stateless services. This design enables fine-grained resource scaling and provides inherent fault tolerance by decoupling compute units. The architecture is powered by a high-performance, CPU-free peer-to-peer communication library that ensures minimal overhead and high throughput. Experiments confirm EaaS's scalability and efficiency, achieving performance comparable to monolithic systems while providing robust fault tolerance and strong scalability. EaaS incurs less than a 2% throughput reduction under simulated hardware failures that would otherwise halt monolithic architectures. It further saves up to 37.5% of computing resources through dynamic fine-grained adaptation to serving traffic, demonstrating strong resilience for large-scale MoE deployment in production.
papers.title_text: Expert-as-a-Service: Towards Efficient, Scalable, and Robust Large-Scale MoE Serving

papers.title: Faithful Prediction of the Performance of rocHPL Despite Hardware and Software Complexity
papers.abstract: High Performance LINPACK (HPL) remains the primary benchmark for ranking supercomputers and often serves as a dimensioning design component for HPC system constructors. Its performance depends on a wide variety of parameters and remains difficult to predict on large, modern, heterogeneous clusters. Using stochastic performance models of computational kernels and the network simulation capabilities of SimGrid, a simulation framework for parallel application performance prediction, we design a lightweight simulator of the open-source implementation of HPL on AMD GPUs (rocHPL). Taking advantage of the structure of HPL, we reduce the simulation complexity by several orders of magnitude. We evaluate the predictive capability of our approach across four distinct accelerated platforms comprising up to 1024 GPUs, two software variants, and a wide range of parameters, and demonstrate its accuracy (simulated and real executions differ by 4% on average), flexibility, and scalability (at this scale, simulations take less than an hour on a laptop).
papers.title_text: Faithful Prediction of the Performance of rocHPL Despite Hardware and Software Complexity

papers.title: FastInfer: Breaking the Low-to-Moderate Sparsity Barrier for Efficient LLM Inference
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to scale, unstructured pruning has become a key technique for reducing inference cost. However, to preserve model quality, pruning is typically limited to low-to-moderate sparsity (30%–60%), where existing GPU-based sparse inference frameworks often fail to deliver consistent speedups over dense baselines. This paper proposes FastInfer, a new sparse LLM inference framework in the low-to-moderate sparsity regime. FastInfer introduces a novel thread-centric encoding paradigm that rethinks sparse computation on Tensor Core Units from the perspective of per-thread register requirements. Based on this, we design the TFBE format, which enables low-overhead operand reconstruction. FastInfer integrates an affinity-aware data-movement mechanism and a triple-stage pipeline to better exploit modern GPU features and improve pipeline utilization. Compared with the state-of-the-art SpInfer, FastInfer achieves geometric-mean speedups of 1.52x (up to 2.1x) for sparse kernels and 1.27x (up to 1.42x) for end-to-end sparse inference on H100.
papers.title_text: FastInfer: Breaking the Low-to-Moderate Sparsity Barrier for Efficient LLM Inference

papers.title: FastMPK: Unleashing Cache Reuse for Sparse Matrix Power Kernels on Many-Core Architectures
papers.abstract: Many applications rely on the sparse matrix power kernel (MPK), which evaluates a short sequence of sparse matrix-vector multiplications (SpMVs) with the same matrix. MPK is therefore dominated by the memory traffic of repeatedly streaming the sparse matrix, and cache reuse across successive SpMVs offers a major opportunity to reduce data movement. However, exploiting such reuse introduces inter-SpMV dependencies that can severely restrict parallelism and induce frequent global synchronization, especially on GPUs. This paper presents FastMPK, a cache-aware MPK designed to run efficiently on both CPUs and GPUs. FastMPK models the matrix as a dependency graph, recursively partitions it into cache-resident subgraphs, and constructs a separator subgraph to decouple cross-subgraph dependencies and recover parallel work. A dependency-preserving runtime schedule maximizes immediate cache reuse while a multi-granularity parallelization strategy enables scalability on many-core processors. Evaluated on diverse architectures, FastMPK delivers average speedups of up to 1.84× over state-of-the-art implementations.
papers.title_text: FastMPK: Unleashing Cache Reuse for Sparse Matrix Power Kernels on Many-Core Architectures

papers.title: FitFloat: Read/Write Random-Access Compressed Floating-Point Arrays for GPUs
papers.abstract: In many floating-point applications that use GPUs, device memory is a bottleneck limiting the maximum problem size. One solution is to use Unified Virtual Memory, but the limited physical GPU memory likely causes page evictions, incurring potentially large performance penalties. We present FitFloat, a drop-in floating-point array replacement supporting user-specified precision on GPUs with the goal of reducing storage requirements of scientific applications while maximizing performance over unified memory. FitFloat targets applications limited by the GPU's memory capacity, allowing larger problem sizes to be efficiently processed. We evaluate the storage savings and performance improvement of our approach relative to using native arrays on 11 single-precision and three double-precision codes from the HeCBench suite on two different GPUs. In the best case, FitFloat yields a speedup of 739 and provides a geometric-mean speedup of 16.1 for the float codes and 20.1 for the double codes on an RTX 4090.
papers.title_text: FitFloat: Read/Write Random-Access Compressed Floating-Point Arrays for GPUs

papers.title: Fluid-Structure Interaction Simulation of Nuclear Reactors with Ultra-Large-Scale Meshes on GPU Clusters
papers.abstract: To overcome mapping bottlenecks and resource underutilization in large-scale nuclear reactor fluid-structure interaction simulations on heterogeneous supercomputers, we propose a GPU-accelerated framework. A matrix-free treecode (MFTC)-RBF strategy is designed to address mapping bottlenecks. It mitigates network latency and synchronization overhead caused by cross-node irregular communication via asynchronous computation-communication overlap. Furthermore, it resolves GPU instruction pipeline stalls induced by transcendental functions using a spatially-decoupled mixed-precision scheme combined with Horner polynomial approximation. To maximize intra-SM resource utilization and throughput, a dual-pipeline asynchronous scheduling (DAS) strategy is adopted to concurrently execute compute-bound and memory-bound tasks on Tensor and CUDA Cores. Evaluations show that MFTC-RBF delivers a 7.08x mapping speedup with scalability across 32,768 GPUs, while DAS hides approximately one-third of DGeMM latency. MFTC-RBF supports state-of-the-art mesh mapping with over 40-billion mesh points. End-to-end benchmarks further demonstrate a ~70% reduction in total runtime. Simulation results closely align with reference data in lead-cooled reactor benchmarks.
papers.title_text: Fluid-Structure Interaction Simulation of Nuclear Reactors with Ultra-Large-Scale Meshes on GPU Clusters

papers.title: FluxZK: Scalable and Efficient Zero-Knowledge Proof Computation via GPU Acceleration
papers.abstract: Zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (zkSNARKs) are a key technology to privacy-preserving applications today. The complexity of proof generation, however, heavily constrains throughput in latency-sensitive environments. The computational burden primarily stems from two fundamental algorithms: Multi-Scalar Multiplication (MSM) and the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT). We propose a series of optimizations for these two kernels, including computation-transfer pipelining, load balancing, and memory access fusion, achieving 1.97 × to 2.16 × proof generation speedup over a state-of-the-art open source GPU acceleration library. Our design also supports out-of-core computation, enabling the generation of large-scale ZKP proofs.

papers.title: FSZ: Breaking the Prediction-Throughput Trade-Off in GPU Lossy Compression
papers.abstract: Existing fast GPU error-bounded lossy compressors have achieved high throughput through pure-GPU single-kernel designs, but their compression ratios remain limited because they typically apply a fixed first-order predictor on independent blocks. We propose FSZ, a GPU error-bounded lossy compressor that redesigns the prediction stage with three mutually reinforcing algorithmic innovations to achieve both higher compression ratios and higher throughput within a single CUDA kernel: (1) cross-block prediction state carries Lorenzo prediction state across block boundaries within 256-element tiles, eliminating 7 out of 8 boundary residuals that inflate encoding rates; (2) per-tile adaptive multi-order prediction and centering adaptively selects the best compression strategy per tile from first-order, second-order, and centering variants; and (3) a single-pass four-way evaluation exploits a mathematical property of finite differences to evaluate all variants from a single data read, enabling richer prediction within the same bandwidth budget as a fixed predictor. Experiments on NVIDIA GH200 GPU with 8 real-world application datasets show that FSZ outperforms cuSZp-P by up to 10.95x and the state-of-the-art cuSZp-O by up to 2.92x in compression ratio. Notably, these gains come with no throughput penalty: FSZ simultaneously achieves the highest average throughput (676 GB/s compression, 785 GB/s decompression) among all evaluated compressors.

papers.title: HCCL: Collective Communication for Meta Training and Inference Accelerators
papers.abstract: We present HCCL, a collective communication library co-designed with Meta's MTIA 300 accelerator, the first Meta chip to integrate backend networking directly on chip package. MTIA 300 includes dedicated message engines (MEs) with near-memory compute (NMC) that fully offload collective execution from the compute grid, enabling large overlap between computation and communication. HCCL uses a compiled communication model in which the host generates a complete description of each collective including dependencies. We describe the control and data path architecture, topology-aware algorithm selection across MTIA 300's asymmetric scale-up and scale-out network, and optimizations for both training and inference workloads. For training, HCCL achieves up to 940 GB/s on intra-rack collectives while introducing less than 0.5% degradation to concurrent compute throughput. For inference, we leverage one-sided communication primitives that bypass the scheduling path to minimize collective latency and describe collective designs that improve compute-communication pipelining for latency-sensitive workloads.
papers.title_text: HCCL: Collective Communication for Meta Training and Inference Accelerators

papers.title: HieraSparse: Hierarchical Semi-Structured Sparse KV Attention
papers.abstract: The deployment of long-context Large Language Models (LLMs) poses significant challenges due to the intense computational cost of self-attention and the substantial memory overhead of the Key-Value Cache (KV Cache). In this paper, we introduce \textit{HieraSparse}, a hierarchical KV Cache compression framework with acceleration kernels that leverage GPU sparse tensor cores to speed up semi-structured KV Cache attention for both the prefill and decode phases. With the hierarchical design, our method allows for a flexible quality-sparsity trade-off and successfully converts sparsity into efficiency. Compared to the state-of-the-art decode method that utilizes unstructured sparsity, \textit{HieraSparse} achieves $\mathbf{1.2\times}$ KV compression ratio and $\mathbf{4.57\times}$ attention speedup at the same sparsity level. Furthermore, we extended the semi-structured KV Cache pruning to the prefill stage, which demonstrated up to $\mathbf{1.85\times}$ attention speedup at the highest sparsity. Lastly, we evaluate the generation quality of \textit{HieraSparse} with a simple magnitude-based pruning method, and the results show that $\mathbf{1.34\times}$ prefill and $\mathbf{1.71\times}$ decode attention speedup can be achieved without significant quality drop. The codebase can be found at https://github.com/psl-ntu/HieraSparse.
papers.title_text: HieraSparse: Hierarchical Semi-Structured Sparse KV Attention

papers.title: High-Performance Tensor Formulation of the Viterbi Algorithm for Hidden Semi-Markov Models
papers.abstract: Hidden Semi-Markov Models (HSMMs) are fundamental probabilistic models widely adopted across diverse domains, from computational biology to finance and signal processing. The Viterbi algorithm decodes the most likely state sequence given an HSMM and can be applied iteratively for ab initio model learning. However, existing Viterbi implementations remain sequential, and GPU-accelerated solutions are entirely absent, making HSMM decoding impractical for large-scale workloads. We present a tensor-based formulation of the Viterbi algorithm for HSMMs, restructuring the inner loops into tensor operations that naturally map onto SIMD units and massively parallel architectures. Building on this formulation, we provide optimized implementations spanning single- and multi-core CPUs, and, for the first time, GPU. Experimental evaluation demonstrates speedups of up to 14x on a single core, over 200x with multi-core, and over 570x on GPU over the state-of-the-art sequential baseline, establishing a new performance baseline for large-scale HSMM decoding.
papers.title_text: High-Performance Tensor Formulation of the Viterbi Algorithm for Hidden Semi-Markov Models

papers.title: Interactive Debugger for Performance-Portable Python HPC Kernels
papers.abstract: We propose PKDB, the first interactive debugger for GPU and multithreaded low-level kernels written in Python. Python is widely used in high performance computing (HPC), with frameworks such as PyKokkos translating Python-embedded domain-specific languages to native code that runs across OpenMP-threaded CPUs and various GPUs. Yet interactive debugging support for such code is absent: developers resort to print statements, framework-specific assertions, or CPU-only execution, the last of which requires altering the program or its data and can mask device-specific bugs. PKDB enables standard interactive debugging like breakpoints, stepping, and variable inspection while preserving actual on-device execution without source modification. Beyond these fundamentals, PKDB introduces two advanced capabilities that exploit the dynamic nature of Python and PyKokkos: (i) Live code evaluation, which lets developers execute arbitrary Python expressions or entire kernels in the middle of a paused kernel without restarting the process; (ii) Kernel call site substitution, which allows an actively running kernel to be updated and reloaded on the fly, so only the kernel is recompiled and re-executed without restarting the application. Our performance evaluation on Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA CPUs, and NVIDIA and AMD GPUs shows that PKDB introduces limited overhead and is practical for everyday use while introducing critical debugging features to the Python HPC ecosystem.

papers.title: LLM-PRISM: Characterizing Silent Data Corruption from Permanent GPU Faults in LLM Training
papers.abstract: Large-scale LLM training is increasingly susceptible to hardware defects stemming from manufacturing escapes and silicon aging. These defects manifest as Silent Data Corruption (SDC) that perturb gradients and parameters throughout the training process. We present LLM-PRISM, a methodology to characterize LLM pre-training resilience to hardware faults. LLM-PRISM couples RTL-level GPU fault simulation with a stochastic injection engine embedded in Megatron-LM. Through 7,664 training runs across FP16, BF16, and FP8 regimes, we analyze how fault type, rate, and numeric format govern resilience. We find that while LLMs resist low-frequency faults, impact is highly non-uniform; critical datapaths and specific precision formats can induce catastrophic divergence even at moderate fault rates. This study provides the first hardware-grounded, pre-training characterization of SDC resilience.

papers.title: MakoXC: Rearchitecting DFT Exchange–Correlation with Matrix-Aligned and Knowledge-Organized Sparsity
papers.abstract: Density Functional Theory (DFT) is indispensable for materials science and drug discovery, yet the exchange--correlation (XC) evaluation remains a major bottleneck due to its cubic scaling. Although linear-scaling methods exploit electronic nearsightedness to reduce asymptotic complexity, they produce irregular sparse workloads that hide implicit sparsity and prevent efficient use of modern AI accelerators. We present MakoXC, a modular matrix-aligned XC evaluation engine that rearchitects nearsightedness-induced sparsity into regular, accelerator-friendly computations. MakoXC co-designs three key techniques: (1) Matrix-Aligned Cells reorganize nearsightedness-induced interactions into dense, accelerator-aligned data clusters; (2) Sparsity-Guided Activation translates deeper implicit sparsity into numerically correct structured execution for practical linear scaling; and (3) Kernel-Fused Pipeline consolidates fragmented workloads into a unified, compute-intensive execution path that fully unleashes accelerator throughput. Extensive evaluations show that MakoXC achieves average speedups of 67.8$\times$ speedup over standard XC evaluation and 4.7$\times$ over state-of-the-art linear-scaling methods. When integrated into a production-grade commercial DFT package, MakoXC scales XC evaluation to ubiquitin (1,231 atoms, def2-SVP) on 64 GPUs, enabling the end-to-end DFT calculation to complete in under five minutes. By restructuring XC evaluation into a unified, structured computation, MakoXC demonstrates how scientific workloads can achieve genuine low complexity while maximizing parallel efficiency on AI accelerators.

papers.title: MIST: A Co-Design Framework for Heterogeneous, Multi-Stage LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Modern LLM serving now spans multi-stage pipelines including RAG retrieval and KV cache reuse, each with distinct compute, memory, and latency demands. Inference engines expose a large configuration space with no systematic navigation methodology, and exhaustively benchmarking configurations can exceed 40K in cloud costs. Simultaneously, the hardware landscape is rapidly diversifying across AMD GPUs, TPUs, and custom ASICs, while cross-vendor prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated configurations lack unified software stacks for end-to-end evaluation today. To address this gap, we present MIST, a Heterogeneous Multi-stage LLM inference Execution Simulator. MIST models diverse request stages; including RAG, KV retrieval, reasoning, prefill, and decode across complex hardware hierarchies. MIST supports heterogeneous clients executing multiple models concurrently unlike prior frameworks while incorporating advanced batching strategies and multi-level memory hierarchies. By integrating real hardware traces with analytical modeling, MIST captures critical trade-offs such as memory bandwidth contention, inter-cluster communication latency, and batching efficiency in hybrid CPU-accelerator deployments. Through case studies, we explore the impact of reasoning stages on end-to-end latency, optimal batching strategies for hybrid pipelines, and the architectural implications of remote KV cache retrieval. MIST empowers system designers to navigate the evolving landscape of LLM inference, providing actionable insights into optimizing hardware-software co-design for next-generation AI workloads.

papers.title: No Disk Left Behind: Lifetime-Aware Oversubscription of Thin Provisioned Storage in Cloud IaaS Platforms
papers.abstract: Cloud resource oversubscription is widely used to improve infrastructure utilization, particularly for CPU resources. In contrast, storage resources remain largely statically provisioned despite significant underutilization. Our analysis of multiple OVHcloud platforms shows that virtual machines use on average only 42.9% of their local disk capacity. In this paper, we explore disk oversubscription in thin-provisioned environments. Unlike CPU, storage resources are persistent and difficult to predict in the black-box context of IaaS platforms. To address these challenges, we introduce Wave, a dynamic oversubscription method that anticipates waves of disk capacity released by Virtual Machine (VM) churn. Using large-scale traces from OVHcloud, we show that Wave can reduce required disk capacity by up to 2× while maintaining a low rate of corrective migrations. Beyond infrastructure efficiency, this reduction translates into significant environmental benefits, lowering storage-related scope 3 emissions by approximately 44.5% in newer cloud regions.
